claim: Mutations in Drosophila Swiss cheese (SWS) gene or its vertebrate orthologue neuropathy target esterase (NTE) lead to progressive neuronal degeneration in flies and humans.
source: Mutations in Drosophila Swiss cheese (SWS) gene or its vertebrate orthologue neuropathy target esterase (NTE) lead to progressive neuronal degeneration in flies and humans.
evidence: This is a well-established finding cited in the abstract and supported by references throughout the manuscript.

claim: NTE/SWS has an enzymatic function as a phospholipase.
source: Despite its enzymatic function as a phospholipase is well established, the molecular mechanism responsible for maintaining nervous system integrity remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract.

claim: NTE/SWS is present in surface glia that forms the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
source: In this study, we found that NTE/SWS is present in surface glia that forms the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and that NTE/SWS is important to maintain its structure and permeability.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: NTE/SWS is important to maintain BBB structure and permeability.
source: In this study, we found that NTE/SWS is present in surface glia that forms the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and that NTE/SWS is important to maintain its structure and permeability.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by permeability assays and structural analyses shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: BBB glia-specific expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS in the sws mutant background fully rescues surface glial organization.
source: Importantly, BBB glia-specific expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS or human NTE in the sws mutant background fully rescues surface glial organization and partially restores BBB integrity, suggesting a conserved function of NTE/SWS.
evidence: This rescue experiment is shown in Figure 2 with quantification in Figure 2H.

claim: BBB glia-specific expression of human NTE in the sws mutant background fully rescues surface glial organization.
source: Importantly, BBB glia-specific expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS or human NTE in the sws mutant background fully rescues surface glial organization and partially restores BBB integrity, suggesting a conserved function of NTE/SWS.
evidence: This rescue experiment is shown in Figure 2D with quantification in Figure 2H.

claim: BBB glia-specific expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS or human NTE in the sws mutant background partially restores BBB integrity.
source: Importantly, BBB glia-specific expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS or human NTE in the sws mutant background fully rescues surface glial organization and partially restores BBB integrity, suggesting a conserved function of NTE/SWS.
evidence: This is shown in the permeability assay data in Figure 4D.

claim: sws mutant glia showed abnormal organization of plasma membrane domains.
source: Interestingly, sws mutant glia showed abnormal organization of plasma membrane domains and tight junction rafts accompanied by the accumulation of lipid droplets, lysosomes, and multilamellar bodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy in Figures 2, 3, and 6.

claim: sws mutant glia showed abnormal organization of tight junction rafts.
source: Interestingly, sws mutant glia showed abnormal organization of plasma membrane domains and tight junction rafts accompanied by the accumulation of lipid droplets, lysosomes, and multilamellar bodies.
evidence: This is shown through Coracle and Neurexin IV staining in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: sws mutant glia showed accumulation of lipid droplets.
source: Interestingly, sws mutant glia showed abnormal organization of plasma membrane domains and tight junction rafts accompanied by the accumulation of lipid droplets, lysosomes, and multilamellar bodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy in Figure 3B-B′.

claim: sws mutant glia showed accumulation of lysosomes.
source: Interestingly, sws mutant glia showed abnormal organization of plasma membrane domains and tight junction rafts accompanied by the accumulation of lipid droplets, lysosomes, and multilamellar bodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Rab7 and CathepsinL staining in Figure 3D-E′′ and quantified in Figure 3F-G.

claim: sws mutant glia showed accumulation of multilamellar bodies.
source: Interestingly, sws mutant glia showed abnormal organization of plasma membrane domains and tight junction rafts accompanied by the accumulation of lipid droplets, lysosomes, and multilamellar bodies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy in Figure 3B-B′.

claim: The observed cellular phenotypes in sws mutants closely resemble characteristics described in lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs).
source: Since the observed cellular phenotypes closely resemble the characteristics described in a group of metabolic disorders known as lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs), our data established a novel connection between NTE/SWS and these conditions.
evidence: This is based on morphological similarities observed in electron microscopy and lysosomal marker accumulation.

claim: A novel connection exists between NTE/SWS and lysosomal storage diseases.
source: Since the observed cellular phenotypes closely resemble the characteristics described in a group of metabolic disorders known as lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs), our data established a novel connection between NTE/SWS and these conditions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: Mutants with defective BBB exhibit elevated levels of fatty acids.
source: We found that mutants with defective BBB exhibit elevated levels of fatty acids, which are precursors of eicosanoids and are involved in the inflammatory response.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GC-MS measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Fatty acids are precursors of eicosanoids.
source: We found that mutants with defective BBB exhibit elevated levels of fatty acids, which are precursors of eicosanoids and are involved in the inflammatory response.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Fatty acids are involved in the inflammatory response.
source: We found that mutants with defective BBB exhibit elevated levels of fatty acids, which are precursors of eicosanoids and are involved in the inflammatory response.
evidence: This is supported by literature citations and the observed correlation with inflammatory markers.

claim: Several innate immunity factors are upregulated in an age-dependent manner as a consequence of a permeable BBB.
source: Also, as a consequence of a permeable BBB, several innate immunity factors are upregulated in an age-dependent manner, while BBB glia-specific expression of NTE/SWS normalizes inflammatory response.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis of AMPs in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: BBB glia-specific expression of NTE/SWS normalizes inflammatory response.
source: Also, as a consequence of a permeable BBB, several innate immunity factors are upregulated in an age-dependent manner, while BBB glia-specific expression of NTE/SWS normalizes inflammatory response.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D where rescue with sws expression reduces AMP levels.

claim: Treatment with anti-inflammatory agents prevents the abnormal architecture of the BBB.
source: Treatment with anti-inflammatory agents prevents the abnormal architecture of the BBB, suggesting that inflammation contributes to the maintenance of a healthy brain barrier.
evidence: This is demonstrated by drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inflammation contributes to the maintenance of a healthy brain barrier.
source: Treatment with anti-inflammatory agents prevents the abnormal architecture of the BBB, suggesting that inflammation contributes to the maintenance of a healthy brain barrier.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of BBB phenotypes by anti-inflammatory drugs.

claim: Aging is the major risk factor for neurodegenerative conditions.
source: Aging is the major risk factor for neurodegenerative conditions, a group of disorders characterized by the progressive degeneration and dysfunction of the nervous system, which includes Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, frontotemporal dementia, and many others.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: Inflammation plays a crucial role in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Growing evidence suggests that inflammation plays a crucial role in age-related neurodegenerative diseases (Zuo et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2018; Rojas-Gutierrez et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Older organisms frequently develop chronic, low-grade inflammation, a condition often named inflammaging.
source: Older organisms frequently develop chronic, low-grade inflammation, a condition often named inflammaging, which is characterized by a sustained increase in inflammatory markers without apparent infection or injury (Chitnis and Weiner, 2017; Franceschi et al., 2018; McGeer and McGeer, 2004; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Inflammaging is characterized by a sustained increase in inflammatory markers without apparent infection or injury.
source: Older organisms frequently develop chronic, low-grade inflammation, a condition often named inflammaging, which is characterized by a sustained increase in inflammatory markers without apparent infection or injury (Chitnis and Weiner, 2017; Franceschi et al., 2018; McGeer and McGeer, 2004; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is the definition of inflammaging supported by citations.

claim: Dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is associated with neuroinflammatory degenerative diseases.
source: One feature associated with neuroinflammatory degenerative diseases is dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) (Takata et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Disruption of the BBB has been observed in patients with numerous neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Disruption of the BBB has been observed in patients with numerous neurodegenerative diseases (Sweeney et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2018; Munji et al., 2019; Blyth et al., 2009; Gray and Woulfe, 2015; Zhou et al., 2023; Whitson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: BBB disruption allows the infiltration of immune cells and molecules that can trigger and sustain inflammatory responses within the brain.
source: Since the BBB plays a crucial role in maintaining the homeostasis of the brain environment, its disruption allows the infiltration of immune cells and molecules that can trigger and sustain inflammatory responses within the brain (Segarra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Dysfunction in lysosomal pathways has been implicated in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease and many other neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Furthermore, dysfunction in lysosomal pathways also has been implicated in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease and many other neurodegenerative disorders (Issa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The lysosome-endosomal system is tightly associated with the maintenance of cell homeostasis and viability, regulation of cell death, oncogenesis, autophagy, and inflammation.
source: The lysosome-endosomal system is tightly associated with the maintenance of cell homeostasis and viability, regulation of cell death, oncogenesis, autophagy, and inflammation (Peng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Dysfunction of lysosomal processes can lead to the accumulation of damaged cellular components and trigger inflammatory responses.
source: Dysfunction of lysosomal processes can lead to the accumulation of damaged cellular components and trigger inflammatory responses, contributing to the overall inflammaging phenomenon (Peng et al., 2019; Aman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Fatty acid metabolism is linked to inflammaging.
source: Fatty acid metabolism is another aspect linked to inflammaging (Calder, 2020; Chew et al., 2020; Emre et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Changes in lipid composition and metabolism, particularly an increase in pro-inflammatory fatty acids, have been observed in inflammaging.
source: Changes in lipid composition and metabolism, particularly an increase in pro-inflammatory fatty acids, have been observed in inflammaging.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the literature.

claim: NTE is a transmembrane protein anchored to the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: NTE is a transmembrane protein anchored to the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum and acts as a phospholipase that regulates lipid membrane homeostasis (Glynn, 2005; Read et al., 2009; Lush et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: NTE acts as a phospholipase that regulates lipid membrane homeostasis.
source: NTE is a transmembrane protein anchored to the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum and acts as a phospholipase that regulates lipid membrane homeostasis (Glynn, 2005; Read et al., 2009; Lush et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Continuous inhibition of NTE activity by the organophosphorus compound tri-ortho-cresyl phosphate causes axonal degeneration in the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS).
source: Continuous inhibition of NTE activity by the organophosphorus compound tri-ortho-cresyl phosphate causes axonal degeneration in the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS), a neuropathy that was consequently named organophosphate-induced delayed neuropathy, OPIDN (Richardson et al., 2013; Richardson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Mutations in the NTE gene cause Gordon-Holmes or Boucher-Neuhäuser syndromes.
source: Moreover, mutations in the NTE gene cause Gordon-Holmes or Boucher-Neuhäuser syndromes (Deik et al., 2014; Synofzik et al., 2014; Synofzik et al., 2015; Topaloglu et al., 2014) and a motor neuron disease called hereditary spastic paraplegia type 39 (HSP 39), in which distal parts of long spinal axons degenerate, leading to limb weakness and paralysis (McFerrin et al., 2017; Rainier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Mutations in the NTE gene cause hereditary spastic paraplegia type 39 (HSP 39).
source: Moreover, mutations in the NTE gene cause Gordon-Holmes or Boucher-Neuhäuser syndromes (Deik et al., 2014; Synofzik et al., 2014; Synofzik et al., 2015; Topaloglu et al., 2014) and a motor neuron disease called hereditary spastic paraplegia type 39 (HSP 39), in which distal parts of long spinal axons degenerate, leading to limb weakness and paralysis (McFerrin et al., 2017; Rainier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: HSP is associated with endo-lysosomal system abnormalities.
source: Over the past few years, research has shown that HSP is associated with endo-lysosomal system abnormalities (Allison et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2015; Namekawa et al., 2007; Renvoisé et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: NTE is widely expressed in the mouse brain.
source: It was shown that NTE is widely expressed in the mouse brain, and its activity is essential for lipid homeostasis in the nervous system (Glynn et al., 1998; Moser et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: NTE activity is essential for lipid homeostasis in the nervous system.
source: It was shown that NTE is widely expressed in the mouse brain, and its activity is essential for lipid homeostasis in the nervous system (Glynn et al., 1998; Moser et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: NTE deficiency results in the distal degeneration of the longest spinal axons, accompanied by swelling that encompasses accumulated axoplasmic material.
source: NTE deficiency results in the distal degeneration of the longest spinal axons, accompanied by swelling that encompasses accumulated axoplasmic material (Read et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Specific deletion of NTE in the neuronal tissue induces neurodegeneration.
source: Specific deletion of NTE in the neuronal tissue induces neurodegeneration (Akassoglou et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: More than 70% of genes related to human diseased are conserved in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, more than 70% of genes related to human diseased are conserved (Ugur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Swiss cheese protein (NTE/SWS) is a highly conserved lysophospholipase that can regulate phosphatidylcholine metabolism.
source: Swiss cheese protein (NTE/SWS) is a highly conserved lysophospholipase that can regulate phosphatidylcholine metabolism (Lush et al., 1998; Zaccheo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: NTE/SWS can act as a regulator of the PKA-C3 catalytic subunit of protein kinase A.
source: It was also shown that NTE/SWS can act as a regulator of the PKA-C3 catalytic subunit of protein kinase A (Bettencourt da Cruz et al., 2008; Wentzell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Loss of Drosophila NTE/SWS and vertebrate NTE results in lipid droplet accumulation.
source: Loss of Drosophila NTE/SWS and vertebrate NTE has been shown to result in lipid droplet accumulation, which is involved in neurodegeneration pathogenesis (Chang et al., 2019; Farmer et al., 2020; Melentev et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Loss of sws leads to age-dependent neurodegeneration.
source: Loss of sws leads to age-dependent neurodegeneration (Figure 1B, arrows), CNS vacuolization, and abnormal glial morphology accompanied by the formation of multilayered glial structures in the adult Drosophila brain (Kretzschmar et al., 1997; Dutta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Loss of sws leads to CNS vacuolization.
source: Loss of sws leads to age-dependent neurodegeneration (Figure 1B, arrows), CNS vacuolization, and abnormal glial morphology accompanied by the formation of multilayered glial structures in the adult Drosophila brain (Kretzschmar et al., 1997; Dutta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Loss of sws leads to abnormal glial morphology accompanied by the formation of multilayered glial structures in the adult Drosophila brain.
source: Loss of sws leads to age-dependent neurodegeneration (Figure 1B, arrows), CNS vacuolization, and abnormal glial morphology accompanied by the formation of multilayered glial structures in the adult Drosophila brain (Kretzschmar et al., 1997; Dutta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pan-glial knockdown of sws leads to increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which in turn induces oxidative stress.
source: Recent studies have shown that the pan-glial knockdown of sws leads to increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which in turn induces oxidative stress (Ryabova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: sws is strongly expressed in the glia that surround the brain and form the blood-brain selective permeability barrier.
source: Importantly, sws was strongly expressed in the glia that surround the brain and form the blood-brain selective permeability barrier (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and F using sws-Gal4 driven CD8::GFP expression.

claim: In Drosophila, the BBB is entirely made by two glial cell layers: PG and SPG.
source: In Drosophila, the BBB is entirely made by two glial cell layers: PG and SPG (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila BBB structure.

claim: SPG cells form a tight barrier that prevents paracellular diffusion and separates the CNS from hemolymph with the help of sophisticated SJs.
source: With the help of sophisticated SJs, SPG cells form a tight barrier that prevents paracellular diffusion and separates the CNS from hemolymph.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila BBB function.

claim: In controls, CoraC is strongly expressed by SPG cells, shown as a smooth line at the brain surface.
source: In controls, CoraC is strongly expressed by SPG cells, shown as a smooth line at the brain surface (Figure 2A, green arrow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upon sws loss, the CoraC pattern at the brain surface was broken and contained lesions and membrane aggregations.
source: Upon sws loss, the CoraC pattern at the brain surface was broken and contained lesions and membrane aggregations (Figure 2B, magenta arrow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: sws mutants showed the formation of various multilamellar bodies in the brain, which were not observed in the control.
source: We found that sws mutants showed the formation of various multilamellar bodies in the brain, which were not observed in the control (Figure 3A–B′).
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 3A-B′.

claim: Multilamellar bodies in sws mutants ranged in size from 5 to 15 μm and contained concentrically laminated and multilayered membranes, lipid droplets, and other partially degraded organelles or cytoplasmic constituents.
source: These atypical structures ranged in size from 5 to 15 μm and contained concentrically laminated and multilayered membranes (yellow arrows), lipid droplets (red arrows), and other partially degraded organelles or cytoplasmic constituents.
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 3B-B′.

claim: The multilamellar inclusions in sws mutants most likely correspond to secondary lysosomes in the phase of digesting endosomal cargo.
source: We hypothesized that these inclusions most likely correspond to secondary lysosomes in the phase of digesting endosomal cargo, which are a hallmark of lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on morphological characteristics and comparison to LSDs.

claim: Rab7 is a small GTPase that belongs to the Rab family and controls transport to late endocytic compartments such as late endosomes and lysosomes.
source: Rab7 is a small GTPase that belongs to the Rab family and controls transport to late endocytic compartments such as late endosomes and lysosomes (Guerra and Bucci, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: In sws-deficient brains, accumulation of Rab7-positive compartments was observed.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated that in contrast to controls, where Rab7 was present in relatively small and evenly dispersed throughout the brain late endosomes and lysosomes (Figure 3D, red), in sws-deficient brains, accumulation of Rab7-positive compartments was observed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D′.

claim: Rab7-positive structures colocalized with atypical membrane aggregates of SPG cells in sws mutants.
source: Moreover, Rab7-positive structures colocalized with atypical membrane aggregates of SPG cells (Figure 3D′, yellow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D′.

claim: CathepsinL is a key lysosomal proteolytic enzyme expressed in most eukaryotic cells.
source: CathepsinL – which is a key lysosomal proteolytic enzyme expressed in most eukaryotic cells (Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: sws loss or its downregulation in barrier-forming glia cells resulted in the appearance of CathepsinL-positive inclusions that colocalized with GFP-labeled membrane aggregates formed in the mutant SPG cells.
source: We found that sws loss or its downregulation in barrier-forming glia cells resulted in the appearance of CathepsinL-positive inclusions that colocalized with GFP-labeled membrane aggregates formed in the mutant SPG cells (Figure 3E–E′′, yellow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E-E′′.

claim: The structures observed upon NTE/SWS deregulation are abnormally enlarged lysosomes.
source: We conclude that the structures observed upon NTE/SWS deregulation are abnormally enlarged lysosomes.
evidence: This conclusion is based on Rab7 and CathepsinL colocalization data.

claim: In mutants with sws loss-of-function and with sws SPG-specific downregulation, a significant increase in the frequency of brains containing Rab7- or CathepsinL-positive aggregates was observed.
source: However, in mutants with sws loss-of-function and with sws SPG-specific downregulation, a significant increase in the frequency of brains containing Rab7- or CathepsinL-positive aggregates was observed (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Analysis of the brains of 15-day-old sws downregulation in SPG cells demonstrated ~2-fold increase in the percentage of brains with lysosomal accumulations within the brain surface in comparison to 1-day-old animals.
source: Analysis of the brains of 15-day-old sws downregulation in SPG cells demonstrated ~2-fold increase in the percentage of brains with lysosomal accumulations within the brain surface in comparison to 1-day-old animals (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3F and G.

claim: NTE/SWS-associated phenotypes might be additionally characterized by the excessive storage of cellular material in lysosomes that is accelerated by age.
source: These data demonstrate for the first time that NTE/SWS-associated phenotypes might be additionally characterized by the excessive storage of cellular material in lysosomes that is accelerated by age.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the age-dependent increase in lysosomal accumulations.

claim: Similar abnormal buildup of cellular material in lysosomes have been found in hippocampal neuropil and spinal axons of NTE-deficient mice.
source: Importantly, similar abnormal buildup of cellular material in lysosomes have been found in hippocampal neuropil (Akassoglou et al., 2004) and spinal axons of NTE-deficient mice (Read et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: NTE/SWS-related phenotypes in mammals may also be associated with excessive storage of cellular material in lysosomes.
source: While these structures have not been specifically described as lysosomal defects, the presence of similar dense bodies containing concentrically laminated and multilayered membranes in NTE-deficient mice suggests that, similar to Drosophila, NTE/SWS-related phenotypes in mammals may also be associated with excessive storage of cellular material in lysosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of structures observed in mice and flies.

claim: LSDs are a group of rare metabolic disorders caused by inherited defects in genes that encode proteins vital for lysosomal homeostasis.
source: LSDs are a group of rare metabolic disorders caused by inherited defects in genes that encode proteins vital for lysosomal homeostasis, such as lysosomal hydrolases or membrane proteins.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: LSDs often manifest as neurodegenerative disorders.
source: LSDs often manifest as neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: In controls, dextran dye predominantly remained at the outer surface of the brain.
source: In controls, dextran dye predominantly remained at the outer surface of the brain (Figure 4B and B′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and B′.

claim: The dye was detected inside almost all of the sws1 mutant brains.
source: In contrast, the dye was detected inside almost all of the sws1 mutant brains (Figure 4C and C′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and C′.

claim: The downregulation of sws in different types of glial cells caused increased permeability of brain barrier in more than 80% of the analyzed brains.
source: Moreover, the downregulation of sws in different types of glial cells also caused increased permeability of brain barrier in more than 80% of the analyzed brains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 4D.

claim: Expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS and human NTE in glia in sws1 mutant partially rescued the barrier phenotype.
source: Expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS and human NTE in glia in sws1 mutant rescued the organization of the surface glia (Figure 2H) and partially rescued the barrier phenotype, suggesting that human NTE and Drosophila NTE/SWS are important for the BBB integrity in Drosophila (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Human NTE and Drosophila NTE/SWS are important for the BBB integrity in Drosophila.
source: Expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS and human NTE in glia in sws1 mutant rescued the organization of the surface glia (Figure 2H) and partially rescued the barrier phenotype, suggesting that human NTE and Drosophila NTE/SWS are important for the BBB integrity in Drosophila (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claim: SPG cells with NTE/SWS deficiency are characterized by defective brain barrier function and lysosomal accumulation of excess cellular material, which includes membranes.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that SPG cells with NTE/SWS deficiency are characterized by defective brain barrier function and lysosomal accumulation of excess cellular material, which includes membranes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the permeability and lysosomal data.

claim: Sodium salicylate and rapamycin showed the best ability to suppress surface glia phenotypes in sws mutants.
source: We revealed that sodium salicylate, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and rapamycin, which activates autophagy by inhibiting Tor (Xu et al., 2017), showed the best ability to suppress surface glia phenotypes in sws mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C′.

claim: An activated inflammatory response is associated with sws deficit.
source: This indicates that an activated inflammatory response is associated with sws deficit.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of anti-inflammatory drugs to suppress phenotypes.

claim: The surface brain layer in moody mutants or upon moody downregulation in SPG contained lesions and had an abnormal membrane assembly, resembling CoraC expression pattern in sws mutants.
source: We observed that the surface brain layer in moody mutants or upon moody downregulation in SPG by moody-Gal4 (moody>moodyRNAi) contained lesions and had an abnormal membrane assembly, resembling CoraC expression pattern in sws mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C and Figure 2B, magenta arrows).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: In moody mutants, the surface glia phenotype could be suppressed by NSAID and rapamycin.
source: We found that in moody mutants, the surface glia phenotype analyzed using CoraC as a marker could also be suppressed by NSAID and rapamycin (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and D′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and D′.

claim: Inflammation, triggered as a result of a compromised brain barrier, plays a role in a feedback loop that exacerbates the abnormal surface glia organization.
source: The fact that anti-inflammatory factors can reduce glial phenotypes in both sws and moody mutants indicates that inflammation, triggered as a result of a compromised brain barrier, plays a role in a feedback loop that exacerbates the abnormal surface glia organization (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is inferred from the drug treatment results and illustrated in Figure 5G.

claim: Inflammation inhibitors only partially rescued the BBB phenotype in moody and sws mutants, suggesting the involvement of additional pathways in maintaining the BBB.
source: At the same time, inflammation inhibitors only partially rescued the BBB phenotype in moody and sws mutants, suggesting the involvement of additional pathways in maintaining the BBB.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue by anti-inflammatory drugs.

claim: The mRNA levels of Attacin A, Cecropin A, and Diptericin were significantly upregulated in sws and moody mutants in comparison to relevant controls.
source: We found that the mRNA levels of all three AMPs were significantly upregulated in mutants in comparison to relevant controls (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR in Figure 5B.

claim: Both mutants with defective BBB exhibit an increased inflammatory response.
source: These data demonstrate that both mutants with defective BBB exhibit an increased inflammatory response.
evidence: This is concluded from the upregulation of AMPs.

claim: Both sws and moody mutants with defective BBB show upregulated levels of linoleic acid, α- and γ-linolenic acid, eicosanoic acid, arachidonic acid, and eicosapentaenoic acid when compared to controls.
source: We found that both mutants with defective BBB show upregulated levels of linoleic acid, α- and γ-linolenic acid, eicosanoic acid, arachidonic acid, and eicosapentaenoic acid when compared to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by GC-MS measurements in Figure 5C.

claim: Levels of 9-cis-tetradecenoic acid, palmitic acid, palmitoleic acid, stearic acid, and oleic acid were elevated upon sws or moody loss.
source: Additionally, levels of other FFAs involved in inflammatory response, 9-cis-tetradecenoic acid, palmitic acid, palmitoleic acid, stearic acid, and oleic acid (Miao et al., 2015; Korbecki and Bajdak-Rusinek, 2019) were elevated upon sws or moody loss (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by GC-MS measurements in Figure 5C.

claim: In both mutants with a compromised BBB, the inflammatory response is accompanied by the accumulation of FFAs.
source: These data show that in both mutants with a compromised BBB, the inflammatory response is accompanied by the accumulation of FFAs.
evidence: This is concluded from the FFA and AMP measurements.

claim: The mRNA levels of Attacin A, Cecropin A, and Diptericin were significantly upregulated in 15- and 30-day-old sws mutants and flies with sws downregulation in SPG cells in comparison to the relevant controls.
source: We confirmed that the mRNA levels of all three AMPs were significantly upregulated in mutants of both ages in comparison to the relevant controls (Figure 5D, black asterisks).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR in Figure 5D.

claim: A significant age-related increase in the expression of inflammatory genes was observed in both sws mutants and flies with sws downregulation in SPG cells.
source: Furthermore, we observed a significant age-related increase in the expression of inflammatory genes in both sws mutants and flies with sws downregulation in SPG cells (moody>swsRNAi, Figure 5D, red asterisks), thereby illustrating the correlation between age-related NTE/SWS neurodegeneration and inflammatory processes.
evidence: This is shown by qPCR in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS in SPG cells in sws1 mutant background normalized levels of inflammatory genes expression in flies of both ages.
source: Importantly, expression of Drosophila NTE/SWS in SPG cells in sws1 mutant background normalized levels of inflammatory genes expression in flies of both ages (15- and 30-day-old flies), confirming that the increased inflammatory response is a consequence of the defective BBB (Figure 5D, green asterisks).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR in Figure 5D.

claim: Downregulating sws in glial cells during adulthood, after BBB formation, resulted in an increased inflammatory response.
source: Moreover, downregulating sws in glial cells during adulthood, after BBB formation, resulted in an increased inflammatory response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Increased levels of AMPs in aging flies with a defective BBB strengthen the connection between the BBB, AMPs, and neuroinflammation.
source: Since previous studies have demonstrated the induction of neurodegeneration by the overactivation of innate immune-response pathways, especially elevated expression of AMPs (Cao et al., 2013), our data showing increased levels of AMPs in aging flies with a defective BBB further strengthen the connection between the BBB, AMPs, and neuroinflammation and reinforce the causative link between BBB breakdown and inflammaging.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by literature citations.

claim: The data reinforce the causative link between BBB breakdown and inflammaging.
source: Since previous studies have demonstrated the induction of neurodegeneration by the overactivation of innate immune-response pathways, especially elevated expression of AMPs (Cao et al., 2013), our data showing increased levels of AMPs in aging flies with a defective BBB further strengthen the connection between the BBB, AMPs, and neuroinflammation and reinforce the causative link between BBB breakdown and inflammaging.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by literature citations.

claim: Macrophages were present within the brain in both developing and adult brains of sws1; srp(Hemo)3xmCherry mutants.
source: In contrast to control brains, we observed the presence of macrophages within the brain in both developing and adult brains of sws1; srp(Hemo)3xmCherry mutants (yellow arrowheads, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Macrophage infiltration into the adult brain was detected in flies with sws downregulation specifically in SPG cells.
source: Moreover, using the anti-NimC1 antibody (Kurucz et al., 2007), macrophage infiltration into the adult brain was detected in flies with sws downregulation specifically in SPG cells (moody>GFP, swsRNAi, yellow arrowheads, Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The presence of an inflammatory response in mutants with a compromised BBB is associated with macrophage entry into the brain.
source: This suggests that the presence of an inflammatory response in mutants with a compromised BBB is associated with macrophage entry into the brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the macrophage infiltration data.

claim: Unlike in sws mutant brains, no intracellular accumulations with extracellular material were observed upon moody loss.
source: Electron microscopy analyses demonstrated that unlike in sws mutant brains, no intracellular accumulations with extracellular material were observed upon moody loss (compare Figure 3B and Bʹ and Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy comparison.

claim: No accumulation of endosomal-lysosomal pathway components such as Rab7 were detected within SPG cells of moody mutants.
source: Furthermore, no accumulation of endosomal-lysosomal pathway components such as Rab7 were detected within SPG cells of moody mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H.

claim: In the absence of moody, SJs were formed, but they were disorganized.
source: At the same time, as previously described (Babatz et al., 2018; Bainton et al., 2005; Schwabe et al., 2005; Li et al., 2021a), we observed that in the absence of moody, SJs were formed, but they were disorganized (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, arrow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F and supported by citations.

claim: Upon sws loss, SJs were not properly assembled and exhibited irregular membrane clusters and disruptions.
source: In comparison to the wild type, upon sws loss, SJs were not properly assembled and exhibited irregular membrane clusters and disruptions (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: The moody mutant exhibited a frayed SJ phenotype.
source: In contrast, the moody mutant exhibited a frayed SJ phenotype (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In-depth examination of cell junctional structures in sws mutants using electron microscopy revealed their improper assembly, characterized by the accumulation of irregular membrane clusters and disruptions in septa organization.
source: The in-depth examination of cell junctional structures in sws mutants using electron microscopy revealed their improper assembly, characterized by the accumulation of irregular membrane clusters and disruptions in septa organization (Figure 6E and F, yellow arrowheads).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Cell junctions are a special type of plasma membrane domain whose transmembrane proteins form a complex, mechanically stable multiprotein structure.
source: Cell junctions are a special type of plasma membrane domain whose transmembrane proteins form a complex, mechanically stable multiprotein structure (Giepmans and van Ijzendoorn, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The lipid component of cell junctions exhibits a typical membrane raft structure.
source: The lipid component of cell junctions exhibits a typical membrane raft structure (Lee et al., 2008; Shigetomi et al., 2023; Nusrat et al., 2000; Simons and Vaz, 2004; Mühlig-Versen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: NTE/SWS influences the composition of membrane rafts.
source: Since NTE/SWS regulates lipid membrane homeostasis, we hypothesized that it influences the composition of membrane rafts.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of NTE/SWS.

claim: Analysis of SPG membranes in sws-deficient brains shows abnormal clustering of SJs proteins and disorganized membrane domains.
source: Analysis of SPG membranes in sws-deficient brains shows abnormal clustering of SJs proteins and disorganized membrane domains, implying that NTE/SWS phospholipase plays a role in organizing SPG membrane architecture (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NTE/SWS phospholipase plays a role in organizing SPG membrane architecture.
source: Analysis of SPG membranes in sws-deficient brains shows abnormal clustering of SJs proteins and disorganized membrane domains, implying that NTE/SWS phospholipase plays a role in organizing SPG membrane architecture (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed membrane disorganization.

claim: The downregulation of Dysb, Npc1a, Pldn, or spin in SPG cells led to abnormal formation of SJs and membrane organization.
source: Significantly, the downregulation of any of these genes led to abnormal formation of SJs and membrane organization in SPG cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: The lysosomal control of membrane homeostasis has a significant impact on the appearance of SJs.
source: This suggests that the lysosomal control of membrane homeostasis has a significant impact on the appearance of SJs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lysosomal gene knockdown experiments.

claim: The phospholipase NTE/SWS plays a crucial role in lysosome biogenesis and organization of the architectural framework of BBB membranes.
source: In summary, our data show that the phospholipase NTE/SWS plays a crucial role in lysosome biogenesis and organization of the architectural framework of BBB membranes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Since NTE/SWS regulates lipid membrane homeostasis, its loss results in the disruption of membrane rafts, which includes SJs, leading to brain barrier permeability.
source: We propose that since NTE/SWS regulates lipid membrane homeostasis, its loss results in the disruption of membrane rafts, which includes SJs, leading to brain barrier permeability.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: As a result of brain barrier permeability, the inflammatory response accompanied by the accumulation of FFAs is activated in mutant brains, leading to progressive neurodegeneration that can be alleviated by the use of anti-inflammatory drugs.
source: As a result, the inflammatory response accompanied by the accumulation of FFAs is activated in mutant brains, leading to progressive neurodegeneration that can be alleviated by the use of anti-inflammatory drugs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data.

claim: The physiological functions of the BBB, maintaining and protecting the homeostasis of the CNS, are evolutionarily conserved across species.
source: The physiological functions of the BBB, maintaining and protecting the homeostasis of the CNS, are evolutionarily conserved across species (Bundgaard and Abbott, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: NTE is highly expressed not only in the nervous system but also in endothelial cells.
source: Interestingly, NTE is highly expressed not only in the nervous system but also in endothelial cells, suggesting that BBB might be affected upon NTE-associated neurodegenerations (The Human Protein Atlas – https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000032444-PNPLA6/single+cell+type).
evidence: This is based on data from the Human Protein Atlas.

claim: BBB might be affected upon NTE-associated neurodegenerations.
source: Interestingly, NTE is highly expressed not only in the nervous system but also in endothelial cells, suggesting that BBB might be affected upon NTE-associated neurodegenerations (The Human Protein Atlas – https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000032444-PNPLA6/single+cell+type).
evidence: This is inferred from NTE expression in endothelial cells.

claim: NTE/SWS is involved in the maturation of non-myelinating Schwann cells during development and de/remyelination after neuronal injury.
source: Considering that NTE/SWS is involved in the maturation of non-myelinating Schwann cells during development and de/remyelination after neuronal injury (McFerrin et al., 2017), it suggests that lysosomal function of NTE/SWS might be essential for proper myelination in vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Lysosomal function of NTE/SWS might be essential for proper myelination in vertebrates.
source: Considering that NTE/SWS is involved in the maturation of non-myelinating Schwann cells during development and de/remyelination after neuronal injury (McFerrin et al., 2017), it suggests that lysosomal function of NTE/SWS might be essential for proper myelination in vertebrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the lysosomal phenotypes and the role in Schwann cells.

claim: Cathepsins have been shown to contribute to neuroinflammation as well as to induce neuronal apoptosis.
source: The most abundant lysosomal proteases, Cathepsins have been shown to contribute to neuroinflammation as well as to induce neuronal apoptosis (Tschopp and Schroder, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: NTE/SWS is crucial for membrane lipid homeostasis, and sws mutants exhibit increased levels of phosphatidylcholine.
source: Previously, it has been demonstrated that NTE/SWS is crucial for membrane lipid homeostasis, and sws mutants exhibit increased levels of phosphatidylcholine (Mühlig-Versen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Phosphatidylcholine possesses an amphiphilic nature, enabling it to energetically self-assemble into continuous bilayers.
source: Phosphatidylcholine, a key component of most organellar membranes, possesses an amphiphilic nature, enabling it to energetically self-assemble into continuous bilayers (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The ability of phosphatidylcholine to spontaneously self-organize can explain the appearance of multilayered membrane structures in the lysosomes of sws mutants.
source: This ability to spontaneously self-organize can explain the appearance of multilayered membrane structures in the lysosomes of sws mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of phosphatidylcholine and the observed phenotypes.

claim: Phosphatidylcholine plays a vital role in generating spontaneous curvature, essential for membrane bending and tubulation in vesicular transport processes within the cell.
source: Furthermore, phosphatidylcholine plays a vital role in generating spontaneous curvature, essential for membrane bending and tubulation in vesicular transport processes within the cell (Epand and Epand, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Abnormal levels of phosphatidylcholine may impact the lysosome fission and fusion steps, leading to the accumulation of defective lysosomes in sws mutants.
source: Therefore, abnormal levels of phosphatidylcholine may impact the lysosome fission and fusion steps, leading to the accumulation of defective lysosomes in sws mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of phosphatidylcholine in membrane dynamics.

claim: Lysosomes are involved in lipid catabolism and transport, and disruptions in their function can affect cellular lipid homeostasis.
source: Since lysosomes are involved in lipid catabolism and transport, disruptions in their function can additionally affect cellular lipid homeostasis (Thelen and Zoncu, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Alterations in lipid composition due to abnormal NTE/SWS phospholipase function and defective lysosomes in sws mutant cells could affect the constitution of the plasma membrane and its ability to form lipid-driven membrane rafts.
source: Consequently, alterations in lipid composition due to abnormal NTE/SWS phospholipase function and defective lysosomes in sws mutant cells could affect the constitution of the plasma membrane and its ability to form lipid-driven membrane rafts.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effects of NTE/SWS loss and lysosomal dysfunction.

claim: Lipid rafts are characterized by the clustering of specific membrane lipids through spontaneous separation of glycolipids, sphingolipids, and cholesterol in a liquid-ordered phase.
source: Lipid rafts are characterized by the clustering of specific membrane lipids through spontaneous separation of glycolipids, sphingolipids, and cholesterol in a liquid-ordered phase (Grassi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Lipid raft assembly dynamics depend on the relative availability of different lipids and membrane proteins.
source: Their assembly dynamics depend on the relative availability of different lipids and membrane proteins (Simons and Vaz, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Tight junctions are considered as raft-like membrane compartments.
source: Interestingly, tight junctions are considered as raft-like membrane compartments (Nusrat et al., 2000), as they represent membrane microdomains crucial for the spatial organization of cell junctions and regulation of paracellular permeability (Lee et al., 2008; Shigetomi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Abnormal organization of tight junctions in the SPG cells of sws mutants is caused by abnormal organization of plasma membrane domains.
source: Therefore, we propose that abnormal organization of tight junctions in the SPG cells of sws mutants is caused by abnormal organization of plasma membrane domains.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data and the nature of tight junctions.

claim: LSDs are often linked to changes in plasma membrane lipid content and lipid raft stoichiometry.
source: LSDs are often linked to changes in plasma membrane lipid content and lipid raft stoichiometry (Domon et al., 2011; Vainio et al., 2005), inflammation (Seehafer et al., 2011; DiRosario et al., 2009), and ER stress responses (Kim et al., 2006; Tessitore et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: LSDs are linked to inflammation.
source: LSDs are often linked to changes in plasma membrane lipid content and lipid raft stoichiometry (Domon et al., 2011; Vainio et al., 2005), inflammation (Seehafer et al., 2011; DiRosario et al., 2009), and ER stress responses (Kim et al., 2006; Tessitore et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: LSDs are linked to ER stress responses.
source: LSDs are often linked to changes in plasma membrane lipid content and lipid raft stoichiometry (Domon et al., 2011; Vainio et al., 2005), inflammation (Seehafer et al., 2011; DiRosario et al., 2009), and ER stress responses (Kim et al., 2006; Tessitore et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Overexpression of human NTE can ameliorate mutant phenotype.
source: However, since we and others Sujkowski et al., 2015 have shown that overexpression of human NTE can ameliorate mutant phenotype, it can be speculated that, depending on the causative mutation, ERT might be an option as treatment of NTE/SWS-related disorders.
evidence: This is supported by the current study and a literature citation.

claim: Depending on the causative mutation, ERT might be an option as treatment of NTE/SWS-related disorders.
source: However, since we and others Sujkowski et al., 2015 have shown that overexpression of human NTE can ameliorate mutant phenotype, it can be speculated that, depending on the causative mutation, ERT might be an option as treatment of NTE/SWS-related disorders.
evidence: This is speculated based on the rescue data.

claim: The ER establishes contacts between its tubules and late endosomes/lysosomes.
source: It has been demonstrated that the ER establishes contacts between its tubules and late endosomes/lysosomes, visualized in unpolarized cells as well as in neurons derived from brain tissue.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Disruption of ER tubules causes accumulation of enlarged and less-motile mature lysosomes in the soma.
source: Moreover, disruption of ER tubules causes accumulation of enlarged and less-motile mature lysosomes in the soma, suggesting that ER shape and proper function orchestrate axonal late endosome/lysosome availability in neurons (Özkan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Abnormal lipid composition in the membrane upon sws loss has a significant effect on lysosome structure and functions.
source: Considering the ER localization of NTE/SWS in the cell, we propose that abnormal lipid composition in the membrane upon sws loss has a significant effect on lysosome structure and functions.
evidence: This is proposed based on the ER-lysosome relationship and NTE/SWS function.

claim: ER forms contact sites with plasma membrane through vesicle-associated membrane protein-associated protein VAP.
source: Furthermore, ER forms contact sites with plasma membrane through vesicle-associated membrane protein-associated protein VAP (Li et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Loss of VAP results in neurodegeneration, such as sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or Parkinson's disease.
source: Loss of VAP results in neurodegeneration, such as sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or Parkinson's disease (Kun-Rodrigues et al., 2015; Anagnostou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Knockdown of sws in neurons reduces mitochondria number in the brain and in wing axons.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of sws in neurons reduces mitochondria number in the brain and in wing axons (Melentev et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: NTE/SWS-deficient animals show activation of ER stress response, characterized by elevated levels of GRP78 chaperone and increased splicing of XBP.
source: NTE/SWS-deficient animals show activation of ER stress response, characterized by elevated levels of GRP78 chaperone and increased splicing of XBP, an ER transcription factor that triggers transcriptional ER stress responses.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Neuronal overexpressing XBP1 and treating flies with tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) alleviated locomotor deficits and neurodegeneration in sws mutants.
source: Neuronal overexpressing XBP1 and treating flies with tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), a chemical known to attenuate ER stress-mediated cell death, alleviated locomotor deficits and neurodegeneration in sws mutants assayed by vacuolization area (Sunderhaus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Reduced levels of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase observed in sws mutants were linked to disrupted lipid compositions.
source: Reduced levels of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase observed in sws mutants were linked to disrupted lipid compositions as well.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Promoting cytoprotective ER stress pathways may provide therapeutic relief for NTE-related neurodegeneration and motor symptoms.
source: Promoting cytoprotective ER stress pathways may provide therapeutic relief for NTE-related neurodegeneration and motor symptoms (Sunderhaus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Drosophila mutants with leaky BBB showed upregulated levels of palmitoleic, oleic, linoleic, linolenic, arachidonic, and eicosapentaenoic acids.
source: We discovered that Drosophila mutants with leaky BBB showed upregulated levels of such fatty acids as palmitoleic, oleic, linoleic, linolenic, arachidonic, and eicosapentaenoic acids, suggesting abnormal metabolism of unsaturated fatty acids upon barrier dysfunction.
evidence: This is shown by GC-MS measurements in Figure 5C.

claim: sws loss results in increased levels of some saturated FFAs, including palmitic and stearic acids.
source: In particular, sws loss results in increased levels of some saturated FFAs, including palmitic and stearic acids.
evidence: This is shown by GC-MS measurements in Figure 5C.

claim: FFAs are known to be significant sources of ROS, which lead to the event of oxidative stress.
source: FFAs or non-esterified fatty acids are known to be significant sources of ROS, which lead to the event of oxidative stress (Soardo et al., 2011), resulting in lipotoxicity associated with ER stress, calcium dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cell death (Ly et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: ROS accumulation and activated ER stress response occur upon sws loss in neurons and glia.
source: Previously it has been demonstrated ROS accumulation and activated ER stress response upon sws loss in neurons and glia (Melentev et al., 2021; Ryabova et al., 2021; Sunderhaus et al., 2019), which might be a result of increased levels of FFAs.
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: ROS accumulation and activated ER stress response upon sws loss might be a result of increased levels of FFAs.
source: Previously it has been demonstrated ROS accumulation and activated ER stress response upon sws loss in neurons and glia (Melentev et al., 2021; Ryabova et al., 2021; Sunderhaus et al., 2019), which might be a result of increased levels of FFAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between FFAs and ROS.

claim: Neuronal sws knockdown results in the upregulation of antioxidant defense genes.
source: In addition, neuronal sws knockdown results in the upregulation of antioxidant defense genes (Melentev et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: BBB breakdown is accompanied by abnormal fatty acids metabolism.
source: We found that BBB breakdown is accompanied by abnormal fatty acids metabolism, and rapamycin can suppress the abnormal glial phenotype formed in BBB Drosophila mutants.
evidence: This is shown by the FFA measurements and drug treatment experiments.

claim: Rapamycin can suppress the abnormal glial phenotype formed in BBB Drosophila mutants.
source: We found that BBB breakdown is accompanied by abnormal fatty acids metabolism, and rapamycin can suppress the abnormal glial phenotype formed in BBB Drosophila mutants.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Saturated FFAs have been shown to lead to target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 activation and cell apoptosis in podocytes.
source: Interestingly, saturated FFAs have been shown to lead to target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 activation and cell apoptosis in podocytes (Yasuda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Rapamycin significantly diminishes FFA-induced podocyte apoptosis.
source: Moreover, rapamycin significantly diminishes FFA-induced podocyte apoptosis (Yasuda et al., 2014), supporting its potential ability to suppress possible outcomes of FFA upregulation in the Drosophila brain, thus improving glial phenotype in mutants with BBB breakdown.
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: PUFAs are known to be primary precursors of lipid mediators that are abundant immunomodulators.
source: PUFAs are known to be primary precursors of lipid mediators that are abundant immunomodulators (Kwon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: PUFAs' metabolism was associated with Alzheimer's disease and dementia.
source: According to published research, PUFAs' metabolism was additionally associated with Alzheimer's disease and dementia (van der Lee et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Chronic inflammatory processes within the CNS are crucial for the development of brain pathologies.
source: The focus of particular interest has recently been on the PUFAs' involvement in the continued inflammatory response because, in contrast to acute inflammation, chronic inflammatory processes within the CNS are crucial for the development of brain pathologies (Regulska et al., 2021; Funk, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: A feedback signaling loop exists between the condition of the brain permeability barrier, lipid metabolism, and the extent of inflammation.
source: Thus, feedback signaling loop exists between the condition of the brain permeability barrier, lipid metabolism, and the extent of inflammation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion illustrated in Figure 5G.

claim: The proportion of older people will increase from one in eight people aged 60 years or over in 2017 to one in six by 2030 and one in five by 2050.
source: As the speed of population aging is accelerating worldwide, the proportion of older people will increase from one in eight people aged 60 years or over in 2017 to one in six by 2030 and one in five by 2050 (Keating, 2022; Rudnicka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: There is little evidence that older people today are in better health than previous generations.
source: Globally, there is a little evidence that older people today are in better health than previous generations (https://www.who.int/home/cms-decommissioning).
evidence: This is cited from WHO.

claim: Most neurodegenerative diseases in humans currently have no cure, and only palliative care is available.
source: Unfortunately, most neurodegenerative diseases in humans currently have no cure, and only palliative care is available.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of inflammaging activated by abnormal fatty acid metabolism may help promote the use of anti-inflammatory therapy and dietary supplements for neurodegeneration.
source: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of inflammaging activated by abnormal fatty acid metabolism and testing new and available drugs in a model organism such as Drosophila may help us to promote the use of anti-inflammatory therapy and dietary supplements for neurodegeneration and get closer to preventing and curing the diseases that lead to malfunctions in the aged brain.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the implications of the research.
